patterns.structure: A number is given in words (millions, thousands, ones with a missing place) and the numeral is asked, or the reverse.
method: Split the words at 'million' and 'thousand'
Write each group as three digits, padding with zeros
Join the groups and check every place has a digit

mistakes.how: Leaves out zero place holders, writing 2 then 6 then 40 as 2 640
Puts 6 thousand in the hundred-thousands place

example.question: Which numeral is 'two million, six thousand and forty'?

patterns.structure: A compound measure (a km b m or a kg b g) is expressed in the larger unit as a decimal, or a decimal is split back into compound form.
method: Convert the small unit to the large unit (m to km, g to kg) using 1000
Write the small part as 3 decimal places, padding with zeros
Add to the whole-number part

mistakes.how: Divides by 10 000 instead of 1000 for the small part

example.question: Express 7 km 85 m in km.

patterns.structure: Four lengths or masses written in different forms (decimal, compound, fraction) must be put in ascending or descending order.
method: Convert every value to the smallest common unit (g or m)
Compare the whole numbers
Re-read the question for lightest-first or heaviest-first

mistakes.how: Reads 2 kg 53 g as 2.53 kg and 2 kg 305 g as 2.305 kg
Orders heaviest to lightest when lightest first was asked

example.question: Arrange from lightest to heaviest: 2.35 kg, 2 kg 53 g, 2 3/5 kg, 2 kg 305 g.

patterns.structure: A fraction or mixed number is expressed as a decimal correct to 1 or 2 decimal places.
method: Divide numerator by denominator
Carry the division one place beyond the rounding place
Round using the digit that follows

mistakes.how: Rounds to 1 d.p. when 2 d.p. asked

example.question: Express 5/9 as a decimal, correct to 2 decimal places.

patterns.structure: Two decimals with different numbers of decimal places are added or subtracted.
method: Write the numbers with the decimal points lined up
Pad the shorter number with zeros
Subtract column by column, borrowing as needed

mistakes.how: In each column takes the smaller digit from the larger, giving 4.63
Forgets to reduce the units digit after borrowing, giving 4.37

patterns.structure: Pick a common multiple or common factor, or find the largest/smallest multiple of n below or above a limit.
method: List multiples of n near the limit, or divide limit by n
Take the whole-number quotient and multiply back
Check against the limit (smaller than vs not more than)

mistakes.how: Picks 200 because it is near, not a multiple
Takes the next multiple above the limit

example.question: Find the largest multiple of 9 that is smaller than 200.
example.solution: 200 / 9 = 22 remainder 2, so 22 x 9 = 198.

patterns.structure: Multiply or divide a fraction/mixed number by a fraction or whole number; answer in simplest form.
method: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions
Change division to multiplication by the reciprocal
Cancel common factors, multiply, convert back

mistakes.how: Takes the reciprocal of the first fraction as well, giving 27/8

example.question: Find 2 1/4 x 2/3. Give your answer in simplest form.

patterns.structure: A fraction of a whole is used; the remainder is shared equally or cut into equal pieces; find the fraction/length per share or the leftover.
method: Subtract the used fraction from 1 to get the remainder
Divide the remainder by the number of shares
For cutting pieces, divide and keep the remainder as leftover

mistakes.how: Divides the fraction eaten (2/7) by 4 instead of the remainder

example.question: Mei ate 2/7 of a cake. Her 4 friends shared the rest equally. What fraction of the cake did each friend get?

patterns.structure: A fixed amount is spent, then a fraction of what remains is spent; a final fraction (or amount) is left; find the original total.
method: Let the original be x or draw a bar model
Find what remains after the fixed amount
Take the second fraction of the REMAINDER, not of x
Equate what is left to the given final fraction/amount
Solve and check by going forward

mistakes.how: Takes 2/5 of the full amount instead of of the remainder
Treats the $36 as the 1/3 left, so total is 3 x 36

example.question: Dev spent $36 on a cap and then 2/5 of the remaining money on shoes. In the end he had 1/3 of his money left. How much money did he have at first?

patterns.structure: One part of a mixture stays the same while the other is added or removed; the part's fraction (or percent) of the whole changes from p to q; find the amount added or the original quantity.
method: Identify the part that does NOT change (heuristic: constant quantity)
Make its units equal before and after (rescale the two ratios)
Compare total units before and after to find the change in units
Match the given amount to those units, then answer the question asked

mistakes.how: Sets 5u = 150 g and gives sauce as 3u
Sets 6u = 150 g and gives sauce as 3u
Gives the final mixture (6u) when sauce mass was asked

example.question: Sauce was 3/5 of a mixture of sauce and meat. After 150 g more meat was added, the sauce was 1/2 of the mixture. What was the mass of the sauce?
example.solution: Sauce stays 3u: before 5u total (3u sauce, 2u meat), after 6u total (3u sauce, 3u meat). Extra meat = 1u = 150 g, so sauce = 3 x 150 = 450 g.

patterns.structure: Two people differ by a fixed amount; each spends a different fraction; they end with equal amounts (or a given difference); find an initial amount.
method: Write the fraction LEFT for each person
Express the larger amount as smaller + difference
Equate remainders (or write the given gap) as a bar model with units
Solve for the unit, then find the quantity asked

mistakes.how: Finds Ahmad's amount (270) instead of Bala's
Divides 90 by 1/6, the difference of the fractions
Gives the $90 gap or the leftover as the answer

example.question: Ahmad had $90 more than Bala. Ahmad spent 2/3 of his money and Bala spent 1/2 of his. They had the same amount left. How much did Bala have at first?
example.solution: Ahmad left = 1/3 of (B+90) = B/3 + 30; Bala left = B/2. B/2 - B/3 = 30 so B/6 = 30 and B = 180. Each has $90 left.

patterns.structure: A fraction relationship (a is p/q of b, or boys are p/q of the group) is converted to a ratio, possibly linking three quantities through a common term.
method: Pick the quantity that appears in both relations as the common term
Give it units so both relations are whole numbers
Read off the ratio in the order asked
Simplify

mistakes.how: Writes pen:ruler:pencil style in the wrong order, giving 3:4:2
Takes the ruler as half of the pen, not half of the pencil

example.question: A pencil costs 3/4 as much as a pen. A ruler costs half as much as the pencil. Find the ratio pen : pencil : ruler.
example.solution: Pen 4u, pencil 3u, ruler 1.5u. Multiply by 2: 8 : 6 : 3.

patterns.structure: Three quantities share a total; relations between them are given as a multiple and as a ratio; find one quantity.
method: Express all three in units using a common term
Add the units and equate to the total
Find one unit then the required quantity

mistakes.how: Reports Ana's share (2 units) instead of Ben's
Uses 'three times' as 3u when Ana is 2u

example.question: Ana, Ben and Cho had 840 stickers. Ben had 3 times as many as Ana. The ratio of Cho's stickers to Ana's was 7 : 2. How many stickers did Ben have?
example.solution: Ana 2u, Ben 6u, Cho 7u; total 15u = 840, u = 56, Ben = 6 x 56 = 336.

patterns.structure: Two or three people share an amount in ratio a:b(:c); some give a fraction/percent/amount to others; the new ratio is given; find an amount or the total.
method: Total is constant, so rescale both ratios to the same total (heuristic: constant total)
Compare each person's units before and after
Match the transferred amount to the difference in units
Find the unit value and the quantity asked

mistakes.how: Gives Mia's amount (48) instead of Noel's
Gives Noel's amount after receiving the money
Compares 4 to 1 in unscaled units, so 3 units = 12 and Noel = 5 x 4

example.question: Mia and Noel had money in the ratio 4 : 5. After Mia gave Noel $12, the ratio of Mia's money to Noel's became 1 : 2. How much did Noel have at first?
example.solution: Total 9 units = 3 units after, so rescale to 36 sub-units: before 16 : 20, after 12 : 24. Mia gave 4 sub-units = $12, so 1 sub-unit = $3 and Noel = 20 x 3 = $60.

patterns.structure: Three groups are in a ratio; on another day two groups change by a percent or fraction while one stays the same; find the new ratio or the new total.
method: Write the first ratio with units
Apply each percent to its own group
Keep the unchanged group's units as is, and write the new ratio
Use a given total (e.g. of two groups) to find 1 unit

mistakes.how: Gives the first-day total of boys and girls

example.question: On Friday, adults : boys : girls at a fair were in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5. On Saturday the number of boys rose by 25% and the number of girls fell by 40%; the number of adults stayed the same. There were 270 boys and girls on Friday. How many people were there on Saturday?
example.solution: Friday boys + girls = 9u = 270, u = 30. Saturday: adults 3u, boys 5u, girls 3u = 11u = 330.

patterns.structure: People pass money/items to each other and spend some; the final amounts are equal or given; find the difference or amount at the start.
method: List the events in order
Start from the end amounts and reverse each event (give becomes add back, spend becomes add back)
Apply reversals in reverse order for each person
Compute the difference asked

mistakes.how: Leaves out the $2 spent, so C started with 7
Subtracts what A gave instead of adding it back
Reports A's starting amount instead of the difference

example.question: Adi, Ben and Cai each ended with $10. Adi gave Ben $4, Ben gave Cai $3, then Cai spent $2. How much more money than Cai did Adi have at first?

patterns.structure: A has d more than B; after A gives B some, A has d' more (or A has k times B); find how many were given or the totals.
method: Note total is constant but the difference changes
Change in difference = 2 x amount given
Divide by 2 for the amount given
If a multiple is given afterwards, use units on the new total

mistakes.how: Gives the change in difference (56) as the amount given

example.question: Pia had 74 more cards than Quin. After Pia gave Quin some cards, she had 18 more cards than Quin. How many cards did Pia give?
example.solution: The gap shrank by 74 - 18 = 56. Each card moves the gap by 2, so 56 / 2 = 28.

patterns.structure: Find a percentage of a quantity, add GST or subtract a discount, express one quantity as a percent of another, or percent change.
method: Identify the base (whole) of the percent
Compute the percent of the base
Add or subtract as the context says
For 'what percent', divide part by base and multiply by 100

example.question: A kettle costs $45 before GST. GST is 9%. How much must Raj pay for the kettle?

patterns.structure: A discounted/increased price (or part) is given with its percent; find the original, the discount in dollars, or a number of items affordable at the original price.
method: Write the given amount as a percent of the original (100% - discount)
Find 1% by dividing
Multiply to get 100% or the percent asked
Use the result in the final step (items, discount %)

example.question: After a 25% discount, a bag cost $63. What was its price before the discount?

patterns.structure: Two groups are related (a multiple or a ratio); each loses its own percent; the total of a third group increases by a stated percent to a given number; find a group's size.
method: Find the third group's original size from its percent change
Find the number who moved (the increase)
Write the number who left as sum of percents of each group in units
Solve for the unit and then the quantity asked

mistakes.how: Reports the smaller club (50) instead of the larger

example.question: The Cooking Club had 5 times as many members as the Chess Club. 20% of the members of each club left to join the Robotics Club. The Robotics Club then grew by 30% to 260 members. How many members did the Cooking Club have at first?
example.solution: Robotics before = 260/1.3 = 200, so 60 joined. 20% of (5c + c) = 1.2c = 60, c = 50. Cooking = 5 x 50 = 250.

patterns.structure: A loan with yearly interest rate is repaid in equal monthly instalments over some years; find the monthly payment or total interest.
method: Interest = principal x rate x years
Total to repay = principal + interest
Divide by the number of months

example.question: Mrs Ong borrowed $48 000 at 5% simple interest per year for 2 years, to be repaid in 24 equal monthly instalments. How much was each instalment?

patterns.structure: A charge has a first-block price and a price for every additional block (or part of one); find the fare/fee for a given distance, weight or time.
method: Subtract the first block from the total quantity
Divide the rest by the block size
Round UP any partial block
Add the first-block charge, plus any waiting/extra fee

mistakes.how: Rounds down 4 blocks plus 10 min to 4 blocks
Counts the first hour again as a block
Charges 7 half-hour blocks from the start

example.question: A car park charges $2.40 for the first hour and $0.70 for every additional half hour or part of it. Zane parked for 3 h 10 min. How much did he pay?
example.solution: Extra time = 2 h 10 min = 4 half-hours + 10 min, so 5 blocks. 2.40 + 5 x 0.70 = 5.90.

patterns.structure: An offer such as 'buy n get 1 free' applies to sets; find the cost of buying a stated number, or how many can be obtained for a budget.
method: Form sets of (n+1) items, each costing n items
Count full sets in the required number
Pay full price for leftover items that do not make a set
Add the costs

mistakes.how: Buys 25 buns (5 sets) and pays for 20

example.question: Buns cost $1.20 each. For every 4 buns bought, 1 bun is free. What is the least amount Lena must pay to get 23 buns?
example.solution: 4 sets of 5 buns = 20 buns cost 16 buns; 3 more buns cost 3. Pay for 19 buns: 19 x 1.20 = 22.80.

patterns.structure: Pieces of fixed length are cut from rolls/bales with no joining; find how many pieces per roll, the least rolls, or the leftover.
method: Divide roll length by piece length: whole number of pieces per roll
Divide the pieces needed by pieces per roll
Round the answer UP
Never use total length / roll length

example.question: Strips 15 cm long are cut from rolls of ribbon, each 100 cm long. No joining is allowed. What is the least number of rolls needed to make 62 strips?
example.solution: 100 / 15 = 6 remainder 10, so 6 strips per roll. 62 / 6 = 10 remainder 2, so 11 rolls.

patterns.structure: Identical pieces are laid in a line with overlaps or gaps (cards, rings, bows, posts); a total length is given; find the number of pieces, or the distance between ends.
method: First piece gives full length; each next piece adds (length - overlap)
Subtract the first piece from the total
Divide by the added length per piece
Add 1 for the first piece (gaps = pieces - 1 for posts)

mistakes.how: Leaves out the +1 for the first piece

example.question: Identical cards, each 10 cm long, are glued in a straight line. Each card overlaps the next by 3 cm. The line is 2.9 m long. How many cards were used?
example.solution: First card 10 cm; each extra card adds 7 cm. (290 - 10) / 7 = 40 extra cards, so 41 cards.

patterns.structure: A block of numbers/shapes repeats; find the sum or the n-th term or the number of a certain shape in the first n terms.
method: Find the cycle length and the sum of one cycle
Divide n by the cycle length: full cycles and remainder
Sum = full cycles x cycle sum + the first 'remainder' terms
Check the remainder terms are from the start of the cycle

example.question: The numbers 2, 5, 1, 4 repeat in this order. What is the sum of the first 90 numbers?

patterns.structure: A sequence of figures grows by an increasing amount; find the count in a later figure, or which figure has a given count.
method: Tabulate the first few figures and the added amount each time
Spot the rule (e.g. add 2, 4, 6... gives n(n+1))
Apply the rule to the figure asked, or solve for n
Check with the figures drawn

mistakes.how: Gives only the amount added in Figure 12

example.question: Figure 1 has 2 squares. Figure 2 has 2 + 4 squares. Figure 3 has 2 + 4 + 6 squares, and so on. How many squares are in Figure 12?
example.solution: Figure n has n(n + 1) squares: 12 x 13 = 156 (= 2 + 4 + ... + 24).

patterns.structure: Find the average of values in a list or table.
method: Add all the values
Divide by the number of values
Include the unit

example.question: Five boys took 14, 17, 12, 13 and 19 minutes to finish a race. What was the average time?

patterns.structure: The average of n values is given with some values known; find the missing value, or the average of a subgroup.
method: Total = average x number of values
Subtract the known values from the total
Divide by the number of unknown values if they are equal
Check the new average

example.question: The average mark of 4 tests is 72. Kai scored 66 in the first test and the same mark in each of the other three tests. What was his mark in each of the other three?

patterns.structure: The average of n different whole numbers (with a digit-length limit) is given; find the largest or smallest possible value.
method: Total = average x n
To make one number largest, make the others as small as allowed AND different
Add the smallest valid distinct values
Subtract from the total and check the digit-length limit

mistakes.how: Gives the sum of the four small numbers

example.question: The average of five different 2-digit whole numbers is 25. What is the largest possible value of one of the numbers?
example.solution: Total = 125. Smallest four different 2-digit numbers: 10 + 11 + 12 + 13 = 46. 125 - 46 = 79.

patterns.structure: A line graph (or table) of volume vs time is shown; read two points to find the rate, a greatest-change interval, or when a target volume is reached.
method: Read values at two clear points on the line
Rate = change in volume / change in time
For a target, find the remaining volume / rate
Add the time to the starting time and convert to clock time

example.question: A tank held 30 L at 10:00 and 90 L at 10:15; the water level rose steadily. The tank holds 150 L. At what time will it be full?

patterns.structure: A tank (given in cm) is part full; a tap fills and a drain empties at the same time; graph or table shows the volume/height at times; find the unknown rate or capacity.
method: Convert dimensions to litres (1000 cm3 = 1 L)
Find initial volume from the fraction filled
Net rate = change in volume / time
Net rate = fill rate - drain rate; solve for the unknown

mistakes.how: Gives the net inflow of 3 L/min

example.question: A tank 60 cm by 50 cm by 40 cm was 1/4 full. A tap running at 5 L per minute filled it while a drain emptied it. After 10 minutes there were 60 L in the tank. What was the drain's rate in L per minute?
example.solution: Capacity = 120 L; start = 30 L. Net gain = 30 L in 10 min = 3 L/min. Drain = 5 - 3 = 2 L/min.

patterns.structure: Distance and time (in minutes or mixed units) are given; find average speed in km/h, or find distance/time from a speed.
method: Convert time to hours (minutes / 60)
Speed = distance / time
Check the unit asked (km/h vs m/min)

example.question: Ravi cycled 9 km in 20 minutes. What was his average speed in km/h?

patterns.structure: Two people travel the same route at different speeds from the same start; one finishes and the other is a distance behind (or ahead); find the later person's finishing time or time difference.
method: Find each person's time for the whole distance (distance / speed)
Convert hours to minutes
Add the time to the start time
Compare finishing times

example.question: Cara and Dev both started running a 4 km route at 07:30. Cara ran at 10 km/h and finished at 07:54. Dev ran at 8 km/h. At what time did Dev finish?

patterns.structure: A figure is made of rectangles and triangles (or one shape inside another); find the shaded/unshaded area by adding or subtracting areas, sometimes using a ratio or half-rectangle fact.
method: Split the figure into rectangles and triangles you can measure
Find any missing side by subtracting known sides
Area of triangle = 1/2 x base x height (height perpendicular to base)
Add or subtract parts as the question requires

mistakes.how: Gives the area of the big triangle
Gives the area of the removed triangle
Uses base x height for both triangles: 540 - 216

example.question: Triangle ABC has a base of 30 cm and a height of 18 cm. A smaller triangle inside it, with base 12 cm on the same line and the same height 18 cm, is unshaded. What is the area of the shaded part?

patterns.structure: A figure is formed from identical triangles/rectangles joined along edges; its area or one perimeter is given; find another perimeter or the area of one piece.
method: Use the given area to find a side (square: side = square root; rectangle: area / side)
Count only the OUTER edges in the perimeter
Check which edges are hidden by joins

mistakes.how: Gives the perimeter of the square only
Reports the area instead of the perimeter

example.question: A square of area 81 cm2 has an equilateral triangle attached on each of its 4 sides. What is the perimeter of the whole figure?
example.solution: Side = 9 cm. The outer boundary has 8 triangle sides of 9 cm: 8 x 9 = 72.

patterns.structure: Identical small rectangles (length = k x width) form a larger figure; the outer perimeter is given; find a side, then the area of the figure or of a part.
method: Let the width be 1u and the length k u
Count how many u make up the outer perimeter (heuristic: units)
Perimeter / total units = 1 unit
Find the dimensions, then the area asked

mistakes.how: Gives the area of one small rectangle
Treats the big figure as a square of side 96/4 = 24

example.question: Six identical rectangles are arranged in 2 rows of 3 to form a bigger rectangle (3 lengths wide, 2 widths tall). Each rectangle's length is 2 times its width. The perimeter of the bigger rectangle is 96 cm. What is its area?
example.solution: Width w: bigger rectangle is 6w by 2w, perimeter 16w = 96, w = 6. Area = 36 x 12 = 432.

patterns.structure: A figure bounded by semicircles/quadrants and straight lines; find its perimeter with a given pi, or in terms of pi.
method: Trace the boundary and list each arc and each straight edge
Arc length = fraction of circle x 2 x pi x r
Do not include edges that are inside the figure (joins)
Add arcs and straight parts, or write as (a pi + b) cm

mistakes.how: Includes the diameter that joins the square and semicircle
Uses the full circumference 44 for the arc

example.question: A semicircle of diameter 14 cm is attached to one side of a square of side 14 cm. Use pi = 22/7. Find the perimeter of the figure.
example.solution: Boundary = 3 sides of the square (42 cm) + semicircle arc (1/2 x 22/7 x 14 = 22 cm) = 64 cm.

patterns.structure: A shaded region lies between squares/triangles and quadrants/semicircles; find its area using a given pi (3.14, 22/7 or calculator).
method: Mark which regions are added and which are subtracted
Find radius from the diameter or side of the figure
Area of quadrant = 1/4 x pi x r x r; semicircle = 1/2 x pi x r x r
Combine and round as the question states

mistakes.how: Uses the arc length 18.84 instead of area

example.question: A quadrant of radius 12 cm is drawn inside a square of side 12 cm, with its centre at one corner of the square. Use pi = 3.14. Find the area of the part of the square outside the quadrant.

patterns.structure: A wheel/ball/tile rolls or is laid along a path; find the number of complete turns, the number of tiles or the length of string around circular objects.
method: Circumference = pi x diameter (convert units first)
Total distance (one way x trips)
Turns = total distance / circumference, whole number for complete turns
For tiles in contact along a path, relate path length to number of diameters

mistakes.how: Doubles for the return trip twice

example.question: A wheel has a diameter of 35 cm. It rolled along a 33 m path and back to the start. Use pi = 22/7. How many complete turns did it make?
example.solution: Circumference = 22/7 x 35 = 110 cm. Distance = 2 x 3300 = 6600 cm. 6600 / 110 = 60.

patterns.structure: A straight line, triangle, isosceles or vertically opposite angle gives the missing angle in one or two steps.
method: Name the fact (angles on a straight line = 180, in a triangle = 180, isosceles base angles equal)
Write the equation
Subtract

mistakes.how: Subtracts only the first angle from 180

example.question: AOB is a straight line. Angle AOC = 118 degrees and angle COD = 35 degrees, where OC and OD both lie on the same side of AB and D is between C and B. Find angle BOD.

patterns.structure: Use properties of a trapezium, parallelogram or rhombus (parallel sides, opposite angles, diagonals) to find an angle, or decide True/False statements about angles.
method: Mark parallel sides; co-interior angles add to 180
Use rhombus/parallelogram facts: opposite angles equal, diagonals of a rhombus bisect angles
Work toward the target angle one fact at a time
For true/false statements, test each with a fact

example.question: ABCD is a rhombus. Angle ABC = 68 degrees. Find angle CAD.
example.solution: Angle BAD = 180 - 68 = 112 (co-interior). The diagonal AC bisects it: 112 / 2 = 56.

patterns.structure: Two or three shapes share a side (rhombus + equilateral/isosceles triangle, rectangle + square, circle with centre O); find an angle that needs 3-5 chained steps.
method: Label every angle you can find directly on the diagram
Use equal sides to get equal angles (isosceles, equilateral = 60)
Move from the shared side to the next shape
Check angles at a point (360) or on a line (180)
Verify the answer is reasonable on the picture

mistakes.how: Gives only the equilateral triangle's angle

example.question: ABCD is a rhombus with angle ABC = 70 degrees. CDE is an equilateral triangle on the other side of CD from A. Find angle ADE.
example.solution: Angle ADC = angle ABC = 70 (opposite angles of a rhombus). Angle CDE = 60. A and E are on opposite sides of DC, so angle ADE = 70 + 60 = 130.

patterns.structure: A paper strip or rectangle is folded along a line; some angles are given; find angles at the fold or in the folded part.
method: A fold is a reflection: the angle before = the angle after on each side of the fold line
Angles on a straight line add to 180
Write an equation using the equal angle twice
Solve and check the other angles

example.question: A strip of paper along line ZAY is folded at A along fold line AB so that AZ lands on AZ' with angle Z'AY = 38 degrees. Find angle ZAB.
example.solution: Angle ZAB = angle Z'AB by the fold. 2 x angle ZAB + 38 = 180, so angle ZAB = 71.

patterns.structure: Shade squares so a figure has a line of symmetry, count lines of symmetry, measure or draw an angle with a protractor, or draw a parallelogram of a given area on a grid.
method: For symmetry, fold along the line: each shaded square needs a mirror partner
Count the squares still missing
For construction, align the protractor baseline and read from the correct scale
For area, count grid squares first

mistakes.how: Counts both diagonals as symmetry lines
Says a rectangle has no symmetry

example.question: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle that is not a square have?
example.solution: One line through the midpoints of each pair of opposite sides. The diagonals are not lines of symmetry.

patterns.structure: A solid built from unit cubes is painted; count cubes with 0, 1, 2 or 3 painted faces, or give surface area, top/side/front views, or nets.
method: Picture or sketch the solid and its layers
Corner cubes have 3 faces painted; edge cubes (excluding corners) 2; face centres 1; hidden cubes 0
Count edge cubes using (edge length - 2) for each edge
Check the counts add up to the total number of cubes

mistakes.how: Gives the number of corner cubes
Gives the cubes with exactly 1 face painted

example.question: A 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm cuboid made of 1-cm cubes has all its outside faces painted. It is then taken apart. How many of the 1-cm cubes have exactly 2 faces painted?
example.solution: Edges of length 4: 4 edges x (4-2) = 8. Edges of length 3: 4 x 1 = 4. Edges of length 2: 4 x 0 = 0. Total 12 (checked by counting all 24 cubes: 8 + 12 + 4 + 0).

patterns.structure: Small and large cubes are packed into a box or built into a bigger cube; find numbers of cubes, side lengths or true/false statements about volumes.
method: Compare side lengths: a cube twice as long has 8 times the volume
Find how many small cubes fit along each edge
The bigger cube's side is the smallest cube that fits the shape
Count cubes needed minus cubes already there

mistakes.how: Builds a 4 x 4 x 4 cube instead

example.question: Twelve identical small cubes are put together to form a cuboid that is 3 cubes long, 2 wide and 2 high. What is the least number of extra small cubes needed to make a bigger solid cube?
example.solution: The smallest cube that contains it is 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 cubes. 27 - 12 = 15.

patterns.structure: A cuboid tank (cm) is full or part full; find volume in litres, extra water to fill, water poured out, a new height, or containers needed.
method: Volume = length x breadth x height in cm3
Convert 1000 cm3 = 1 L (1 cm3 = 1 mL)
Use the fraction/height given for part-full
For containers, divide and round UP

example.question: A tank 50 cm long, 40 cm wide and 30 cm high is 3/4 filled with water. The water is poured into bottles, each holding 1.2 litres. How many bottles are needed to hold all the water?
example.solution: Capacity = 60 000 cm3 = 60 L. Water = 3/4 x 60 = 45 L. 45 / 1.2 = 37.5, so 38 bottles.

patterns.structure: Read volumes from measuring containers or labelled bottles in mL and L and combine them.
method: Read each scale carefully (what does one division stand for?)
Convert all to the same unit
Add or subtract
Express in the unit asked

mistakes.how: Keeps the sum of mL but labels it L

example.question: Three containers hold 350 mL, 0.8 L and 1 1/4 L of water. What is the total volume in litres?

patterns.structure: Add or subtract a duration to a clock time (12-hour or 24-hour), find the duration between two times, or convert minutes to hours.
method: Break the duration into hours and minutes
Add (or subtract) the hours, then the minutes
Carry 60 minutes into an hour
Check a.m./p.m.

example.question: A film started at 9:45 a.m. and lasted 2 h 50 min. At what time did it end?

patterns.structure: A weekly routine (different savings on weekdays and weekends) repeats; find how many days to reach a target.
method: Find the saving each weekday and each weekend day
Find the saving in one full week
Subtract full weeks from the target and then count the remaining days one by one
Count the days in the full weeks plus the extra

mistakes.how: Divides 52.80 by the average 3 per day and rounds up
Stops at the end of the weekdays

example.question: Ken gets $6 pocket money every day. From Monday to Friday he spends $4.20 each day; on Saturday and Sunday he spends none. He starts saving on a Monday. After how many days will he first have at least $52.80?
example.solution: Week saves 5 x 1.80 + 2 x 6 = 21. Two weeks (14 days) = 42. Next Mon-Fri adds 9 = 51 (day 19). Saturday adds 6 = 57, so day 20.

patterns.structure: Simplify a linear expression, or find its value for a given number.
method: Group like terms (same letter, same power)
Keep the sign in front of each term
Substitute the number in place of the letter
Evaluate using order of operations

example.question: Express 6k + 9 - 2k - 4 in its simplest form.

patterns.structure: A situation uses letters for unknown amounts (stickers, strawberries, pages); write and simplify an expression for a total or a remainder, then evaluate it.
method: Write each quantity in terms of the letter
Decide whether to add or subtract for each event
Simplify like terms
Substitute a given value if asked

example.question: Lia had (4n + 3) stickers. She gave 2n stickers to Mei and then bought 5 more. Express the number of stickers Lia has now in terms of n.

patterns.structure: Sides of a figure are written as expressions in x and the perimeter is given; find x and then a side or the area.
method: Add all sides and simplify
Set equal to the perimeter
Solve the linear equation
Substitute back to find what is asked

mistakes.how: Reports x instead of the longest side

example.question: A triangle has sides (2x + 3) cm, (x + 5) cm and 3x cm. Its perimeter is 44 cm. What is the length of the longest side?

patterns.structure: A job is shared equally by some workers; some are absent so the rest do n more each; find the total in terms of n.
method: Let each worker's original share be c
Total = original workers x c = remaining workers x (c + n)
Solve for c in terms of n
Total = workers x c

example.question: 24 workers were to pack the same number of cartons each. 3 workers were absent, so each of the others packed n more cartons. Find the total number of cartons in terms of n.
example.solution: 24c = 21(c + n), so 3c = 21n and c = 7n. Total = 24 x 7n = 168n.

patterns.topic: Reasoning (true / false / not possible to tell)
patterns.structure: Statements about a situation, algebraic expressions or a figure must each be marked True, False or Not possible to tell.
method: Decide what is known for sure and what depends on unknown values
Test each statement with a general fact, or with two different values
If two values give different answers, it is NOT possible to tell
Check angle/volume statements against a property

mistakes.how: Assumes x = 10, so 'A holds more' looks True
Tests x = 1 only and says False
Says 3x is always more than x + 8

example.question: Tank A holds 3x litres and Tank B holds (x + 8) litres. Statement 1: Together they hold (4x + 8) litres. Statement 2: Tank A holds more than Tank B. Mark each True, False or Not possible to tell.
example.solution: 3x + x + 8 = 4x + 8, true. 3x > x + 8 only if x > 4, which is not known.

patterns.structure: A table, bar graph or picture graph is given; read values and find a total, difference, fraction/percent of a total, or decide which statement is true.
method: Read the scale first (what does each gridline stand for?)
List the values
Find the total or difference
Fraction/percent = part / total

mistakes.how: Divides 54 by the other three days (114)
Divides by the number of days (4)

example.question: Oranges sold: Monday 36, Tuesday 48, Wednesday 30, Thursday 54. What fraction of all the oranges were sold on Thursday?

patterns.structure: A bar/line graph gives some values; an average or total is stated; find the missing value, or a related value from a second graph.
method: Total = average x number of values
Add the values you can read
Missing value = total - known values
Use it to answer the next part (percent, comparison)

mistakes.how: Reports the sum of known values
Uses average x 3 as the total

example.question: A bar graph shows the number of cakes sold on four days: Monday 24, Tuesday 30, Thursday 18, and Wednesday (bar missing). The average number sold per day was 25. How many were sold on Wednesday?

patterns.structure: A rate (items per minute, cost per gram) is given for a small amount; find the amount for a larger time/quantity.
method: Find the rate per 1 unit (divide)
Multiply by the new quantity
Check units

example.question: A machine makes 18 cups in 6 minutes. At this rate, how many cups does it make in 45 minutes?
example.solution: 18 / 6 = 3 cups per minute. 3 x 45 = 135.

patterns.structure: Two machines/pumps do the same job in different times; their rates differ by a stated amount per minute; find a rate, the job size or the time together.
method: Same job: faster time and slower time give a ratio of rates (inverse)
Use units: rate ratio and the given difference
Find each rate and the job size
Combined time = job / (sum of rates)

example.question: Pump A fills a tank in 40 minutes and Pump B fills the same tank in 60 minutes. Pump A pumps 5 litres more per minute than Pump B. If both run together, how many minutes do they take to fill the tank?
example.solution: Rates are in ratio 3 : 2, so A is 1 unit more = 5 L/min. B = 10 L/min, A = 15 L/min, tank = 600 L. 600 / 25 = 24 min.

patterns.structure: Equal (or related) numbers of two items at different unit prices; the difference in total spent is given; find the number of items or each price.
method: Find the price difference for one pair
Total difference / price difference per pair = number of pairs
If numbers differ by a fixed amount, first remove the extras and their cost
Use the number to answer the question

example.question: Ben bought the same number of pens at $3.40 each and pencils at $1.15 each. He spent $38.25 more on pens than on pencils. How many pens did he buy?
example.solution: Each pair costs 3.40 - 1.15 = 2.25 more for the pen. 38.25 / 2.25 = 17.

patterns.structure: The same total is shared in two ways (one leaves a surplus, the other a shortage); find the number of people and the total.
method: Write the total two ways in terms of the number of people
Equate and solve for the number of people
Substitute back for the total
Check both ways

example.question: If each child gets 7 sweets, there are 12 sweets too few. If each child gets 4 sweets, there are 18 left over. How many sweets are there?

patterns.structure: Two kinds of item with different counts per item (legs, wheels, cost); the total number of items and total value are given; find how many of each (assumption method or guess and check).
method: Assume all items are the type with fewer per item
Compute the total under that assumption
Difference from the real total / difference per item = number of the other type
Check the totals

example.question: A shop had tables (4 legs each) and stools (3 legs each): 18 pieces with 62 legs altogether. How many tables were there?
example.solution: If all were stools: 54 legs. 62 - 54 = 8 extra legs, each table adds 1, so 8 tables (10 stools).

patterns.structure: Items are bought or built in fixed combinations (1 cake + 6 cookies, 1 car + 1 bicycle); a total cost/count is given; find the number of sets or of one item.
method: Form one group (set) and find its cost/count
Total / cost of a set = number of sets
Multiply by the number of each item per set if the question asks for items

example.question: A cake costs $9 and a cookie costs $2.50. Hana bought 6 cookies for every cake and spent $144 in all. How many cakes did she buy?
example.solution: One set = 1 cake + 6 cookies = 9 + 15 = $24. 144 / 24 = 6 sets, so 6 cakes.

patterns.structure: A container with identical items has a total mass; after removing some items the mass changes; find the mass of one item or of the empty container.
method: Mass removed = difference between the two total masses
Mass of one item = mass removed / number removed
Subtract items' total from the whole to find the container

mistakes.how: Reports the mass of the 10 removed apples
Reports the mass of one apple
Reports the mass of all apples

example.question: A basket with 25 identical apples has a mass of 4.9 kg. After 10 apples are removed, the mass is 3.1 kg. What is the mass of the empty basket?
example.solution: 10 apples = 1.8 kg, so 1 apple = 0.18 kg and 25 apples = 4.5 kg. Basket = 4.9 - 4.5 = 0.4 kg.

patterns.structure: Squares (or similar rectangles) have sides in a ratio; a difference or total of areas is given; find an area or a side.
method: Square the side ratio to get the area ratio
Express the given area difference or total in area units
Find 1 area unit, then the area asked
Take the square root if a side is needed

mistakes.how: Treats 5 - 2 = 3 units as the area difference

example.question: The sides of two squares are in the ratio 2 : 5. The area of the bigger square is 63 cm2 more than the area of the smaller. What is the area of the smaller square?
example.solution: Areas are in ratio 4 : 25. 21 units = 63, 1 unit = 3. Smaller = 4 x 3 = 12.

patterns.structure: Two quantities are given (sometimes in different units) and their ratio is asked in simplest form, or a missing term of an equivalent ratio is found.
method: Write the quantities in the order the question names them, in the same unit
Divide both terms by their highest common factor
For a missing term, find the multiplier between the known terms and apply it to the other side

mistakes.how: Writes the difference 15 as a part of the ratio

example.question: Tom has 45 stickers and Lena has 60 stickers. Find the ratio of Tom's stickers to Lena's stickers in its simplest form.
example.solution: The highest common factor of 45 and 60 is 15. 45 : 60 = 3 : 4.

patterns.structure: Triangles stand on the same straight line and share the same top vertex, so their areas are in the ratio of their bases; the ratio of two areas and another area (a total or a bigger triangle) are given.
method: Spot the common height: same top vertex, bases on one line
Turn the area ratio into a ratio of bases and units
Match the given area to the correct number of units, then find the unit value
Multiply by the units of the triangle asked

mistakes.how: Gives the area of the smaller triangle (3 units)
Reports the given total area as the answer
Divides 96 by the 5 units of SQR instead of the 8 units of SPR

example.question: P, Q and R lie on one straight line, in that order, and S is a point above the line. Triangle SPQ and triangle SQR have areas in the ratio 3 : 5. The area of triangle SPR is 96 cm². Find the area of triangle SQR.
example.solution: Triangles SPQ and SQR share the height from S. SPR is made of both, so it is 3 + 5 = 8 units = 96 cm², 1 unit = 12 cm². SQR = 5 x 12 = 60 cm².

patterns.structure: Two quantities are in ratio a : b; some of one quantity is sold, spent or added while the other stays the same; the new ratio is given and an amount or a total is asked.
method: Mark the quantity that does not change and give it the same number of units before and after
Rescale the two ratios so the unchanged quantity has equal units
Compare the changing quantity before and after; the unit difference equals the amount removed or added
Find one unit, then the quantity asked

mistakes.how: Gives the cookies at first instead of the brownies

example.question: A box held cookies and brownies in the ratio 7 : 4. After 40 cookies were sold, the ratio of cookies to brownies became 1 : 2. How many brownies were in the box?
example.solution: Brownies stay at 4 units. After the sale, cookies : brownies = 1 : 2 = 2 : 4, so cookies = 2 units. Sold = 7 - 2 = 5 units = 40, 1 unit = 8. Brownies = 4 x 8 = 32.

patterns.structure: Two quantities each gain or lose the same amount; the difference between them stays fixed; the new ratio is given and the amount (or an original value) is asked.
method: The difference between the quantities does not change, so use it as the constant
Turn the difference of the new ratio into units
Find the unit value and the new amount of either quantity
Subtract the original amount to find the change

mistakes.how: Gives Ali's new amount instead of the amount added

example.question: Ali had $75 and Ben had $45. Each of them then received the same amount of money and the ratio of Ali's money to Ben's money became 5 : 4. How much did each of them receive?
example.solution: The difference stays at 75 - 45 = $30. In 5 : 4 the difference is 1 unit, so 1 unit = $30 and Ali has 5 x 30 = $150. Ali received 150 - 75 = $75.

patterns.structure: Two or three quantities are in a ratio and one of them is a stated amount more than another; find a single quantity or the total.
method: Write the ratio as units
Match the stated difference to the difference in units
Find one unit
Multiply by the units needed (one part or all parts)

mistakes.how: Gives the stated difference as the total
Adds 7 + 4 units but uses the difference per unit of 4

example.question: Mei and Jun shared some stickers in the ratio 7 : 4. Mei had 36 more stickers than Jun. How many stickers did they have altogether?
example.solution: The difference is 7 - 4 = 3 units = 36, so 1 unit = 12. Total = 11 x 12 = 132.

patterns.structure: A fraction of a whole is used or sold first; the rest is shared in a three-part ratio; one share is given and the original whole is asked.
method: Find the units for the remainder from the three-part ratio and the given share
Convert the remainder into a fraction of the whole (1 minus the fraction used)
Equate the remainder to its fraction and scale up to the whole

mistakes.how: Stops at the remainder after selling
Treats the 150 as 2/5 of the whole instead of 3/5
Adds the sold fraction to the remainder as a number

example.question: Mrs Lee baked some tarts and sold 2/5 of them. The rest were packed into boxes A, B and C in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5. Box B had 45 tarts. How many tarts did she bake?
example.solution: Box B is 3 units = 45, so 1 unit = 15 and the 10 units for the rest = 150. The rest is 3/5 of all tarts, so 3/5 of the total = 150, 1/5 = 50 and total = 250.

patterns.structure: Fractions with unlike denominators are compared or put in order; a fraction between two others or the greatest/smallest is chosen.
method: Find a common denominator (or turn each into a decimal)
Compare the numerators over the common denominator
Pick out the fraction asked and write it in its original form

mistakes.how: Treats the fraction with the smallest denominator as the smallest
Picks the second smallest after a slip

example.question: Which of the following fractions is the smallest? 3/4, 5/8, 2/3, 7/12

patterns.structure: A measured quantity (kg, litres, metres) is bought and a fraction of it is used; the amount used or the amount left is asked, often as a mixed number.
method: Find the fraction left (1 minus the fraction used) if the left-over is asked
Multiply the quantity by that fraction
Change the improper fraction to a mixed number if the options are mixed numbers

mistakes.how: Finds the amount used and stops
Subtracts 2/5 from 3 kg as if both were kg
Leaves 9/5 and picks the wrong option form

example.question: Aisha bought 3 kg of flour and used 2/5 of it to bake. How much flour did she have left?

patterns.structure: A whole is split by a fraction into two kinds; a fraction of one kind and a number of the other are sold; the amount left is given and the original total is asked.
method: Write each kind as a fraction of the total
Work out the fraction of the total left in each kind
Add the fractions left, take away the fixed number sold, and equate to the amount left
Solve for the total (unit fraction method)

mistakes.how: Forgets the 40 raisin buns sold, so 7/10 of T = 100

example.question: A baker made some buns. 2/5 of them were cheese buns and the rest were raisin buns. He sold 3/4 of the cheese buns and 40 raisin buns and had 100 buns left. How many buns did he make?
example.solution: Cheese left = 1/4 of 2/5 = 1/10 of the total. Raisin = 3/5 of the total, so raisin left = 3/5 - 40. 1/10 + 3/5 = 7/10, so 7/10 of the total - 40 = 100, 7/10 of the total = 140 and the total = 200.

patterns.structure: A mixed number is written as an improper fraction (or the reverse), or an equivalent fraction with a stated denominator is chosen.
method: Multiply the whole number by the denominator
Add the numerator
Keep the denominator; check by dividing back

mistakes.how: Uses only the whole number times the denominator

example.question: Which fraction is equal to 3 2/7?

patterns.structure: A figure is divided into equal parts with some shaded; the fraction shaded or unshaded is asked in simplest form.
method: Count the equal parts in all
Count the parts asked for (shaded or unshaded)
Write part over whole and simplify

mistakes.how: Gives the shaded fraction in simplest form

example.question: A rectangle is divided into 24 equal parts and 9 parts are shaded. What fraction of the rectangle is not shaded? Give your answer in simplest form.
example.solution: Unshaded parts = 24 - 9 = 15. 15/24 = 5/8.

patterns.structure: A fraction of one quantity equals a different fraction of another; their ratio is found, then a total or difference is used to find one amount.
method: Give the equal parts the same number of units (make both equal to a common multiple of the numerators)
Read each quantity in units and form the ratio
Use the total or difference to find one unit
Multiply to find the amount asked

mistakes.how: Takes the ratio as 3 : 2 from the numerators, so 1 unit = 51 and Sam = 2 units
Uses 3 : 2 and reads Sam as the 3 units

example.question: 3/4 of Ravi's savings is equal to 2/3 of Sam's savings. Together they have $255. How much does Sam have?
example.solution: Let 3/4 of Ravi = 2/3 of Sam = 12 units. Ravi = 12 / (3/4) = 16 units and Sam = 12 / (2/3) = 18 units, so Ravi : Sam = 8 : 9. 17 units = 255, 1 unit = 15, Sam = 9 x 15 = $135.

patterns.structure: A fraction of a whole (a pizza, a cake, a rope) is shared equally among some people or cut into equal slices; the fraction of the whole for each is asked.
method: Treat sharing equally as division: fraction divided by the number of shares
Multiply the denominator by the number of shares
Simplify and check the answer is a fraction of the whole, not of the part

mistakes.how: Divides the whole by 6 only, ignoring the 3/4

example.question: 3/4 of a pizza was shared equally among 6 people. What fraction of the whole pizza did each person get?

patterns.structure: The same amount of a bottle, tank or packet is used each day; the fraction left is given at two different days; find the amount used per day or the day it runs out.
method: Subtract the two fractions left to get the amount used between the two days
Divide by the number of days between them to get the amount per day
Divide the whole (1) by the daily amount for the total days, or the fraction left by it for days still to go

mistakes.how: Gives the days still needed after day 10 (3/8 divided by 1/16)
Adds 4 + 6 and says the bottle is empty
Divides 3/4 by 1/16 and gives the days after day 4

example.question: Dev used the same amount of juice from a bottle every day. At the end of day 4, 3/4 of the bottle was left. At the end of day 10, 3/8 of the bottle was left. On which day was the bottle empty?
example.solution: Used in 6 days = 3/4 - 3/8 = 3/8, so 1/16 per day. The whole bottle lasts 1 / (1/16) = 16 days.

patterns.structure: A length or volume (often a mixed number) is cut or poured into pieces of a fractional size; find how many pieces or the leftover.
method: Change mixed numbers to improper fractions
Divide by multiplying by the reciprocal of the piece size
Check the answer is a count of pieces (a whole number, or a leftover shown separately)

mistakes.how: Divides the piece size by the total

example.question: A ribbon 2 1/4 m long is cut into pieces that are each 3/8 m long. How many pieces are there?

patterns.structure: A fraction of a group has one description and the rest another; the numbers differ by a stated amount; find the whole group (or one part).
method: Write both parts as fractions of the whole
Subtract the fractions and match the difference to the stated number
Find the unit fraction, then the whole

mistakes.how: Reports the stated difference as the total
Finds the children instead of the total
Finds the adults instead of the total

example.question: 3/7 of the passengers on a bus were children and the rest were adults. There were 48 more adults than children. How many passengers were on the bus?
example.solution: Adults = 4/7, children = 3/7, so the difference is 1/7 = 48. The whole = 7 x 48 = 336.

patterns.structure: One quantity is expressed as a fraction (or percentage) of another, usually in different units, in simplest form.
method: Change both quantities to the same unit
Write the first over the second
Simplify

mistakes.how: Writes the 2 m over the 35 cm

example.question: Express 35 cm as a fraction of 2 m in simplest form.

patterns.structure: A multi-digit multiplication, division, addition or subtraction is done without a calculator (no story).
method: Set out the working place by place
Break the multiplier into easy parts (25 = 20 + 5)
Check by estimating

example.question: Find the value of 4 056 x 25.

patterns.structure: An expression with brackets and mixed operations is evaluated; the order brackets, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction decides the answer.
method: Work out the brackets first
Do multiplication and division from left to right
Do addition and subtraction from left to right

example.question: Find the value of 48 - 6 x (3 + 2) + 20 / 4.

patterns.structure: A number is rounded to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand (or decimal place), or a calculation is estimated by rounding each number first.
method: Underline the digit in the place being rounded to
Look at the digit to its right: 5 or more rounds up
Replace all later digits with zeros

mistakes.how: Drops the digits instead of rounding

example.question: Round 48 752 to the nearest thousand.
example.solution: The thousands digit is 8 and the next digit is 7, so round up: 49 000.

patterns.structure: The place or the value of a digit in a decimal is asked, or a decimal is read as a number of tenths, hundredths or thousandths.
method: Count places to the right of the decimal point: tenths, hundredths, thousandths
Write the value as a decimal or fraction
Do not confuse the place name with the digit

example.question: What is the value of the digit 4 in 7.0845?
example.solution: 7 . 0 8 4 5: tenths 0, hundredths 8, thousandths 4. The value is 4 thousandths = 0.004.

patterns.structure: Decimals with different numbers of places are ordered, or a decimal between two others is chosen.
method: Write every decimal with the same number of places
Compare digit by digit from the left
Put in order or pick the one asked

mistakes.how: Thinks 5.309 is bigger than 5.31 because it has more digits
Picks the number above the upper limit

example.question: Which number lies between 5.31 and 5.4? 5.309, 5.35, 5.41 or 5.039
example.solution: As thousandths: 5.310 < 5.350 < 5.400. 5.350 lies between them, so the number is 5.35.

patterns.structure: A decimal is added, subtracted, multiplied or divided by a whole number or a power of ten, with no story.
method: Ignore the decimal point and calculate
Count the decimal places in the question
Put the point back in the answer, adding zeros if needed

mistakes.how: Puts the point one place too far left
Puts the point one place too far right
Forgets a factor of 100 when multiplying by 500

example.question: Find the value of 3.64 x 500.

patterns.structure: All the given digits are used once to form the largest or smallest number with a condition (even, odd, a multiple).
method: List what the last digit must be for the condition (even, odd, multiple of 5)
Put the other digits in the order that makes the number smallest or largest
A number cannot start with 0

mistakes.how: Orders digits from largest to smallest

example.question: Use all the digits 3, 0, 7 and 5 once to form the smallest 4-digit even number.
example.solution: The only even digit is 0, so the number ends in 0. The other digits 3, 5, 7 in increasing order give 3 570.

patterns.structure: Three people (or items) have a total; one has a stated amount more than another and another has a multiple; find one amount using unit bars.
method: Pick the smallest quantity as 1 unit
Express the other quantities as units plus the stated extra
Subtract the extra from the total and divide by the units to find 1 unit
Work out the quantity asked

mistakes.how: Divides the total by 4 units without removing $35

example.question: Ken, Lee and May saved $435 altogether. Lee saved $35 more than Ken. May saved twice as much as Ken. How much did Lee save?
example.solution: Ken = 1 unit, Lee = 1 unit + $35, May = 2 units. 4 units + 35 = 435, 4 units = 400, 1 unit = $100. Lee = 100 + 35 = $135.

patterns.structure: Two people differ by a fixed number of years; after some years one age is a multiple of (or equals a total with) the other; find an age now.
method: The age difference never changes
Draw bars for the ages after the stated years
Match the difference to the units difference, then find one unit
Subtract the years to get the age now

mistakes.how: Gives the son's age after 6 years
Adds the 6 years to the mother only: S + 36 = 4S

example.question: Mrs Tan is 30 years older than her son. In 6 years' time, her age will be 4 times her son's age. How old is her son now?
example.solution: In 6 years the difference is still 30 years = 3 units, so 1 unit = 10 years. Son in 6 years = 10, so now = 10 - 6 = 4.

patterns.structure: Two purchases share one item and differ in the other (3 books and 2 pens vs 3 books and 5 pens); the totals are given; find the price of one item.
method: Line up the purchases so one item has the same number
Subtract the totals; the difference is the cost of the extra items
Divide to get the price of one item
Substitute back to find the other price

mistakes.how: Reports the cost of the 3 extra pens
Gives the price of one book

example.question: 3 notebooks and 2 pens cost $13. 3 notebooks and 5 pens cost $19. Find the cost of one pen.
example.solution: The second purchase has 3 more pens and costs 19 - 13 = $6 more. 3 pens = $6, so 1 pen = $2.

patterns.structure: Coins or notes of two values are in a stated relationship (twice as many, 3 more); their total value is given; find the number of one kind.
method: Convert all values to the same unit (cents or dollars)
Find the value of one set of the related coins
Divide the total by the value of one set
Use the relationship to find the kind asked

mistakes.how: Uses the 18 dollars as a count

example.question: Sana had twice as many 50-cent coins as 20-cent coins. The total value of her coins was $18. How many 20-cent coins did she have?
example.solution: 1 twenty-cent coin with 2 fifty-cent coins = 20 + 100 = 120 cents. 1 800 / 120 = 15 sets, so 15 twenty-cent coins.

patterns.structure: A mass, length or volume in mixed units (kg and g, km and m) is used and topped up in a short story; the amount now or left is asked in one unit.
method: Change every amount to the same unit (all in kg or all in g)
Follow the story: subtract what was used, add what was bought
Give the answer in the unit asked

mistakes.how: Stops after subtracting the amount used

example.question: Mrs Goh had 3 kg 250 g of rice. She used 1.8 kg of it and then bought 750 g more. How many kilograms of rice did she have then?

patterns.structure: The volume of a cuboid or cube is found from its sides, or a missing side (height, edge) is found from a stated volume.
method: Write volume = length x breadth x height
Substitute the known sides
For a missing side divide the volume by the product of the other sides

example.question: A cuboid has a square base of side 6 cm and a volume of 288 cm3. Find its height.
example.solution: Base area = 6 x 6 = 36 cm2. Height = 288 / 36 = 8 cm.

patterns.structure: A solid or box is built from 1-cm cubes; the volume or the number of extra cubes to fill or complete it is asked.
method: Count cubes in one layer, then multiply by the number of layers (or use length x breadth x height)
Subtract the cubes already there when more are needed
Volume in cm3 equals the number of 1-cm cubes

mistakes.how: Gives the volume of the box and ignores the cubes already in it
Adds the 20 cubes to the volume

example.question: A box measures 6 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm. It already contains 20 one-cm cubes. How many more 1-cm cubes are needed to fill the box completely?
example.solution: Box volume = 6 x 4 x 3 = 72 cm3, which holds 72 cubes. 72 - 20 = 52 more cubes.

patterns.structure: A solid is named from its faces, edges or vertices, or a net is chosen or completed for a cube, prism or pyramid.
method: Count and name the faces (shape and number)
Match the faces to a solid: prism, pyramid, cube, cuboid
For a net, imagine folding it and check no two faces land on each other

mistakes.how: Picks a prism for 1 square and 4 triangles
Picks the cube because of the square face

example.question: A solid has 1 square face and 4 triangular faces. What is the name of the solid?
example.solution: A pyramid has one base and triangular faces meeting at a point. A square base with 4 triangles is a square-based pyramid.

patterns.structure: The shape with a stated property (one pair of parallel sides, equal diagonals, all sides equal) is named from a list, or the property of a named shape is tested.
method: Recall the properties of each shape in the options
Test each option against the property
Choose the only one that fits exactly

mistakes.how: Picks the rhombus, which has two pairs
Picks the rectangle, which has two pairs

example.question: Which shape has exactly one pair of parallel sides? rhombus, trapezium, kite or rectangle
example.solution: A rhombus and a rectangle have two pairs of parallel sides. A kite has none. A trapezium has exactly one pair.

patterns.structure: The height that goes with a stated base of a triangle (inside a figure of several triangles) is named, before using base x height / 2.
method: The height is perpendicular to the base and ends at the opposite vertex
Look for the right-angle mark
Extend the base line if the foot of the height is outside the triangle

mistakes.how: Picks a part of the base

example.question: In triangle PQR, QR is the base. Point S is on QR and PS is perpendicular to QR. Which line is the height that goes with the base QR?
example.solution: The height meets the base at a right angle. PS is perpendicular to QR, so it is the height.

patterns.structure: A person facing a compass direction (or an object on a grid) turns through a stated angle clockwise or anticlockwise; the new direction or the object faced is asked.
method: Place the starting direction on the 8-point compass (each step is 45 degrees)
Turn clockwise by adding, anticlockwise by subtracting
Read the new direction

mistakes.how: Reads 135 degrees as a compass bearing

example.question: Jay was facing north-east. He turned 135 degrees clockwise. Which direction was he facing then?
example.solution: North-east is 45 degrees from north. 45 + 135 = 180 degrees from north, which is south.

patterns.structure: A pie chart shows parts of a whole as sectors (angles or percentages); the number in a sector, or a fraction of the total, is found.
method: Write the sector as a fraction of the whole: angle over 360 (or percentage over 100)
Multiply by the total
Compare sectors by their angles

example.question: A pie chart shows the favourite sport of 240 students. The football sector is 90 degrees. How many students chose football?
example.solution: 90/360 = 1/4 of the students chose football. 1/4 x 240 = 60.

patterns.structure: A figure of equal parts has some shaded; the percentage shaded or unshaded is asked, or a figure with a stated percentage shaded is chosen.
method: Count equal parts in all and the parts asked for
Write part over whole and scale to 100
Check shaded and unshaded add to 100 per cent

mistakes.how: Treats the 26 unshaded parts as 26 per cent
Gives the shaded count as a percentage

example.question: A figure is made of 40 equal squares. 14 squares are shaded. What percentage of the figure is not shaded?

patterns.structure: A sum is deposited in a bank paying a yearly interest rate; the interest or the total after some years is asked (simple interest unless stated).
method: Interest for 1 year = rate per cent of the deposit
Multiply by the number of years
Add the deposit if the total amount is asked

example.question: Mr Ong put $8 000 in a bank that pays 2.5% simple interest per year. How much money did he have in the bank after 3 years?

patterns.structure: Two people or vehicles travel at different speeds, towards each other or one after the other; when and where they meet, or how far apart they are, is asked.
method: Towards each other: add the speeds; one after the other: subtract them
Time to meet = gap / combined (or relative) speed
Distance of each = own speed x time

mistakes.how: Gives the distance from B (Raj's distance)
Gives the time to meet in hours

example.question: Town A and town B are 280 km apart. At the same time, Tom drove from A towards B at 60 km/h and Raj drove from B towards A at 80 km/h. How far from town A did they meet?
example.solution: They close the gap at 60 + 80 = 140 km/h, so they meet after 280 / 140 = 2 h. Tom drove 60 x 2 = 120 km from A.

patterns.structure: Numbers are written in a table with a few columns (often reversing direction on alternate rows); the column or row of a large number is found.
method: Find the repeat length (the number of columns) and the direction of each row
Divide the number by the number of columns to find its row
Use the remainder and the row's direction to find the column

mistakes.how: Reads an odd row from the right
Rounds the row up and picks the last column
Picks the first column of the row

example.question: The numbers 1, 2, 3, ... are written in 4 columns A to D. Row 1 reads A to D as 1 to 4. Row 2 goes the other way, from D to A, as 5 to 8. Rows keep going left to right, then right to left. In which column is 50?
example.solution: 50 / 4 = 12 remainder 2, so 50 is the 2nd number in row 13. Odd rows run from A to D, so the 2nd number is in column B.

notes: frequency = number of distinct papers (of the 209 listed) in which the pattern was observed. Every paper was OCR'd with Tesseract; patterns also keep the papers from the earlier 20-paper pass, whose evidence is merged into seenIn.

OCR is good for question text but noisy for symbols, fractions and diagrams. Pages that failed OCR (images) and questions garbled beyond recognition are not counted, so frequencies are still lower bounds.

Questions were split from OCR text and assigned to patterns by keyword rules, then spot-checked by sampling; the split is imperfect (a block can hold more than one question, one question can be cut). Of 6428 question blocks, 5062 were assigned to a pattern and 1366 were left unclassified (unmatched, sub-parts without context, or too garbled). Cover pages, instruction pages and answer-key/solution pages were excluded before counting.
Some newer patterns have low frequencies because their keywords are narrow, not because they are rare.
exampleWrongAnswer on a mistake is the wrong value that mistake produces for the pattern's own example (usable as a distractor).
